📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.S. space economy.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding.

This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U.S. Moon Base. Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads.

Recent findings suggest that NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases.

Recent findings suggest that the new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions.

The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1.3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies.

Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards:.

An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon.

This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments.

Elementium Materials Inc., selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars.

It has been revealed that A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure. The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads.

Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
  • In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
  • Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, mentioned it was shelving intends to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

Recent findings suggest that "We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot.".

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation.".

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

According to recent reports, many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

It has been revealed that china's EV-makers can bring a upcoming model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security.".

PwC remarked Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those fresh technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

It has been revealed that wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

According to recent reports, domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

Sources indicate that in Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000.".

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

For Germany, the problem isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany.".

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light. Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast.

It has been revealed that rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io. He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years.

Sources indicate that to his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

It has been revealed that rømer figured out the pattern and made an accurate prediction for Io's eclipse on Nov. 9, 1676. Then on Nov. 21, he took his findings to the Royal Academy of Sciences and explained that a finite speed of light must be responsible.

Understanding that the speed of light is a constant is the key that opened our ability to gauge the scale of the universe, as well as was central to developing modern physics."The speed of light becomes a sort of ultimate speed limit," Live Science explained in an article about why the speed of light matters. "In fact, objects with mass, be they cars or neutrinos, can't reach the speed of light because they would need infinite energy to do so.".

#93364. Industry News: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (793 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means.
  • Industry observers note that the study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations.
  • "What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," claims Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. New research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

Industry observers note that the study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," claims Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

According to recent reports, members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

Sources indicate that these contrasting perspectives may have important consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to latest evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science.

Dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

The researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

According to recent reports, both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

Some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as new challenges arise.

It has been revealed that dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Why the Public Sees Science Differently.

Another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

According to recent reports, one possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

It has been revealed that the differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when new evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery.

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

It has been revealed that with researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

The study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

"Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she notes. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.".

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: Cruising through the outer solar system, the Voyager 2 spacecraft made its closest approach to Neptune on August 25, 1989, the only spacecraft to visit the most distant ice giant planet. Based on the images recorded during its close encounter and in the following days, this inspired composited scene covers the dim outer planet, largest moon Triton, and faint system of rings. From just beyond Neptune's orbit, the interplanetary perspective looks back toward the Sun, capturing the planet and Triton as thin sunlit crescents. Cirrus clouds and a dark band circle Neptune's south polar region, with a cloudy vortex above the pole itself. Parts of the very faint ring system along with the three bright ring arcs were first imaged by Voyager during the fly-by, though the faintest segments are modeled in this composited picture. Spanning 7.5 degrees, the background starfield is composed from sky survey data centered on the constellation Camelopardalis, corresponding to the outbound Voyager's view of the magnificent Neptunian system. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Death adds to national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years.

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 ⁠on Friday, involving a child who tested positive for the infectious disease, the state’s health department said.

It has been revealed that the department stated the child was ⁠age four or younger. It did not disclose additional details, including the child’s vaccination status, citing the family’s privacy.

The death adds to a worsening national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years.

Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases as of Friday.

Wisconsin has ⁠also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated ​death, involving a ​child.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed six ​measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not ​specify the states ‌where the deaths were ​recorded.

A discrepancy between ​state and federal death tallies arose after the CDC, under the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

Virginia has reported 220 measles ⁠cases so far in 2026, including 40 among children four years old or younger and 75 among those age five to 12, state ⁠health department data showed as of Thursday.

Of those cases, 179 involved unvaccinated individuals, 39 were associated with people ‌whose vaccination status was ‌unknown and two occurred with vaccinated individuals.

Industry observers note that “Virginia has not had a measles-related death ‌since 1978,” stated Frederic Bertley, immunologist and chief executive officer of the Center of Science and Industry. Sources indicate that virginia health officials have reported increased measles activity driven largely by outbreaks ‌in the state’s central region. Buckingham county has reported 127 cases, the most in the state, while neighboring Charlotte county has recorded 34 ​cases.

#93358. Breaking: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1112 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.
  • The limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD.
  • Recent findings suggest that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.

The limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD. However, a large Latin cross carved into its lid dates to approximately the 10th or 11th century, suggesting that the person buried inside lived hundreds of years after the coffin was originally made.

Recent findings suggest that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation. The remains likely belong to a prominent medieval monk, and researchers have narrowed the possible identities to two men who once led Westminster Abbey.

Two Medieval Abbots Emerge as Leading Candidates.

The new findings, published in the peer-reviewed Journal of the British Archaeological Association, come from Professor Warwick Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Recent findings suggest that rodwell identifies Aelfwig, an abbot who died around 1020, as the strongest candidate. At the time, Westminster Abbey was a Benedictine monastery, and Aelfwig had served there as a monk before becoming its abbot.

Recent findings suggest that another possibility is Wulnoth, who succeeded Aelfwig and died in 1049. Both men are believed to have been buried at the Abbey, making either a plausible match for the skeleton.

"We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," says Professor Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Recent findings suggest that "We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to fifty when he died.

"The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.".

The elaborate burial provides another reason to suspect that the deceased held an important position. Rodwell suggests that the individual was 'honored' with a 'fine sarcophagus', an unusual distinction that would be consistent with the status of an abbot.

Recent findings suggest that rather than commissioning an entirely fresh stone coffin, those responsible for the burial apparently reused an existing Roman sarcophagus. The man's wooden coffin was placed inside it, and the stone lid was modified with a prominent Latin cross. This may represent an early example of recycling a valuable object for an entirely different purpose.

New Excavations Reveal the Skeleton's Age.

The Roman sarcophagus and its mysterious occupant have fascinated researchers for generations. Rodwell's latest conclusions draw on several investigations conducted with specialists over the years, including work associated with Channel 4's Time Team.

In 2009, the television program examined the archaeology and architecture of King Henry III's original sacristy, located along the north side of Westminster Abbey.

According to recent reports, the same area was the scene of an earlier accidental discovery in 1820, when workers encountered the Roman coffin and broke its lid into six pieces. The damage was repaired around the time the sarcophagus was formally 'discovered' in 1869.

Industry observers note that more recently, Pre-Construct Archaeology, one of the UK's largest commercial archaeological and heritage organizations, carried out another excavation of the sacristy. Completed in 2025, the project was undertaken to support construction of the King Charles III Sacristy, a fresh facility at Westminster Abbey scheduled to open the following year.

As part of this investigation, human bone specialist James Young Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology (PCA) conducted a fresh examination of the skeleton.

According to recent reports, his analysis indicated that the deceased was a man between 35 and 49 years old who stood approximately 5 feet 9 inches tall. These findings differ considerably from an assessment made in the 1800s, which described the remains as those of a 'robust young man' no older than 30 and approximately 5 feet 7 inches tall.

Carbon Dating Confirms a 1,000-Year-Old Burial.

In a recent development, one of the most notable clues came from scientific dating of the remains. A bone sample was submitted to the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre for radiocarbon analysis, which produced a date range of 987 to 1052 AD.

This places the burial firmly within the late Saxon period, centuries after the Roman sarcophagus was originally created. The dates also align with the deaths of both Aelfwig and Wulnoth, strengthening the case that the skeleton belonged to one of these medieval abbots.

"This confirms that the reuse of the sarcophagus, and the associated remodeling of its cover, occurred in the late Saxon period.".

The results provide scientific support for the theory that an ancient Roman burial container was repurposed to honor an vital religious figure nearly 1,000 years ago.

A Skeleton Thought Lost Was Hiding in Plain Sight.

It has been revealed that the investigation also brought renewed attention to an unexpected discovery made in 2016. For years, researchers had believed that the skeleton was missing, leaving an important part of the burial's history unresolved.

Sources indicate that that assumption proved mistaken when the sarcophagus was transported to a conservation studio. PCA researchers removed its lid and were surprised to find an almost complete human skeleton still inside.

Recent findings suggest that the examination produced another clue that Rodwell describes as a 'remarkable latest discovery'. Inside the stone coffin, researchers identified the rectangular outline of a structure that had disappeared long ago. Its shape was preserved by a white residue left behind by lime, a material historically used in burials.

Rodwell believes the outline marks the position of the original wooden coffin that held the deceased before it was placed inside the Roman sarcophagus.

"Although no physical traces of that feature remained, it can only have been a timber coffin, which has completely decayed over the course of the seven centuries that the sarcophagus was buried in the sacristy courtyard," writes Professor Rodwell.

Together, the rediscovered skeleton, evidence of a wooden coffin, and new scientific dating have transformed researchers' understanding of this unusual burial. Although the man's identity has not been established beyond doubt, the findings suggest that a medieval abbot may have been laid to rest in a Roman coffin already centuries old.

Visitors can see the sarcophagus today in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.

French government minister Marlene Schiappa has come under fire from members of her own party after appearing on the front cover of Playboy magazine.

Schiappa, who has been a government minister since 2017, appeared on the cover of the magazine to accompany a 12-page interview she did on women’s and LGBT rights. Schiappa, who is the current Minister for the Social Economy and French Associations, was photographed for the cover wearing a white dress.

Sources indicate that schiappa has been a long-time advocate for women’s rights and was appointed as the country’s first ever Gender Equality Minister in 2017. In this role, she successfully spearheaded a latest sexual harassment law which allows for on the spot fines to be issued to men who catcall, harass or follow women on the street.

Her appearance has drawn criticism from political colleagues including French Prime Minister Elisabeth Borne.

Borne pulled up Schiappa over the cover, telling her it “wasn’t appropriate, especially during this period,” CNN affiliate BFMTV reported Saturday, citing a source close to the prime minister.

France is currently in the throes of a political and social crisis triggered by French President Emmanuel Macron’s move to push ahead with controversial pension reforms despite widespread public opposition.

“We are in the middle of a social crisis, there is the issue of policing, there are people between life and death, and I have the impression of being behind a smoke screen,” Sandrine Rousseau, Green Party politician and fellow women’s rights activist, told BFMTV Friday.

France wracked by more pension protests amid rising violence on the streets.

French politician, Jean Luc Mélenchon who came third in the 2022 presidential elections criticized both Schiappa’s appearance and the decision by French President Emmanuel Macron to give an interview to children’s magazine, Pif Gadget, this week.

Sources indicate that “In a country where the President expresses himself in Pif and his minister in Playboy, the problem would be the opposition. France is going off the rails,” Mélenchon tweeted Saturday.

Schiappa responded to her critics in a tweet on Saturday, saying: “Defending the right of women to have control of their bodies, that’s everywhere and all the time. In France, women are free. With all due respect to the detractors and hypocrites.”.

French Interior Minister, Gérald Darmanin came to Schiappa’s defense during an interview with French news channel CNews on Sunday calling her a “woman of character.”.

“I wanted to say that Marlene Schiappa is a courageous female politician who has her character and who has her style which is not mine, but I respect,” he remarked.

Breaking: Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training.
  • Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on complications that matter to them, such as climate protection.
  • What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a substantial city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on complications that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today.".

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," indicates Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests.".

Recent findings suggest that the 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

In a recent development, UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

It has been revealed that nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30.".

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," claims Brod.

In a recent development, he is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an key step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

In a recent development, "Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," indicates Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

In a recent development, her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have stated 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US vice-president claims it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim.

At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Donald Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to obtaining a nuclear weapon in February that it was essential for the US to go to war with the Islamic republic.

In the White House briefing room, Trump was asked about reporting this week that he was unhappy with the US vice-president’s statement blaming Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war.

Industry observers note that “I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” Trump said. “I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that if it were asked, I would have said that: ‘Would you do it again?’ And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”.

However, Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to developing a nuclear weapon this year that it was necessary to go to war, which he has made dozens of times in the past nine months, is undermined by public evidence and contradicts his own previous statements on US strikes against Iranian facilities in 2025.

At a campaign rally in Alaska last month, Trump insisted that he had to join Israel in attacking Iran in February because, “they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”.

In a recent development, that claim appears at odds with what his then director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, testified to Congress on 25 March 2025, two months into Trump’s second term: that US intelligence agencies reported that Iran had not tried to make a nuclear weapon for more than two decades. The US intelligence community, Gabbard said, “continues to assess Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and supreme leader Khamenei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003”.

According to recent reports, despite that assessment, three months later, on 21 June 2025, Trump ordered the US bombing of Iran’s nuclear enrichment facilities. The strikes, Trump told the public that night, “were a spectacular military success. Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.”.

Eight months after that, however, when Trump announced the start of a full-scale war on Iran early on 28 February 2026, he said in a video statement from Mar-a-Lago the war was necessary to “ensure that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon”.

The morning after this month’s midterm elections, Vance stated in a statement posted on social media: “The reason we lost is the war.”.

Sources indicate that “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he added. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost.”.

In the White House briefing room on Friday, after Trump said that Vance should have said the war was necessary, a reporter asked the vice-president whether he would argue that the war in Iran was worth it.

In his response, Vance said it was not his place to second-guess the president, but refrained from actually endorsing Trump’s claim that the war was essential to stop Iran from creating a nuclear weapon.

Sources indicate that “Look, what I’ve said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It’s the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, of innocent people,” Vance said. “I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again.”.

“My view is that my goal is, and my job is, to support the president of the United States,” the vice-president said.

The vice president’s office did not respond to a request to comment.

Industry News: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, newly introduced observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole.
  • Industry observers note that the center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment.
  • In a recent development, over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, newly introduced observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole. An international research team led by MPE has traced these compact clouds to a massive pair of stars whose powerful winds appear to produce material that could eventually help feed the black hole, known as Sagittarius A*.

Industry observers note that the center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment. At its core sits Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), a supermassive black hole surrounded by stars, gas, and dust moving through a region dominated by intense gravitational forces. This extreme setting gives astronomers an opportunity to investigate how matter moves near black holes and where the material that sustains their activity comes from.

In a recent development, over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*. These mysterious "clumps" may provide notable clues about how material makes its way toward the black hole. However, scientists have struggled to determine where the clouds originate and what causes them to form.

Mysterious Gas Clouds Near the Milky Way's Black Hole.

One of the first major discoveries came in 2012, when astronomers identified a compact cloud of ionized gas called G2. Containing several times Earth's mass, the cloud produces emissions from hydrogen and helium, consistent with hot gas mixed with dust. It follows a highly elongated orbit around Sagittarius A* and has a faint extension trailing behind it, known as G2t.

In a recent development, soon afterward, researchers examining older observations recognized another similar object, G1, traveling along a closely related path. The similarities suggested that G1, G2, and G2t might not be independent objects. Instead, they could represent concentrations of gas within a larger, continuous stream.

Even relatively small differences in gas density can make such a stream appear broken into separate clouds. This happens because the brightness of the gas increases in proportion to the square of its density, making denser regions stand out much more strongly.

Industry observers note that more recently, astronomers observed gas in G2's trailing material gathering into another compact cloud that follows a similar orbit. Although this newly formed object might naturally be called G3, that designation had already been assigned to a different object. Together, the related clouds trace a connected flow of material through the Galactic Center, known as the G1-2-3 streamer.

These clouds could play a surprisingly crucial role in sustaining the black hole. Calculations suggest that if approximately one Earth mass of gas reaches Sagittarius A* every ten years, it could provide enough fuel to maintain the black hole's current level of activity. Discovering how the clouds form could therefore help explain how the black hole receives its supply of matter.

Astronomers Trace the Gas Clouds to Their Source.

Researchers have considered several possible explanations for the clouds, including powerful winds from massive stars, stellar explosions such as novae, and gas pulled away from objects by the black hole's gravity.

Industry observers note that to investigate, the MPE-led team used two advanced infrared spectrographs, SINFONI and ERIS. Both instruments employ adaptive optics to produce sharper observations. By examining a specific hydrogen emission feature called the Brackett‑γ line, the astronomers measured the clouds' positions and velocities and reconstructed their paths around Sagittarius A*.

According to recent reports, the results revealed a striking pattern. G1, G2, and G2t all follow orbits with nearly the same shape and orientation. It would be extraordinarily unlikely for three unrelated clouds to share such closely matching orbital characteristics, strongly suggesting that they originated from the same source.

Two Massive Stars May Be Creating the Clouds.

By working backward from the clouds' observed motions and their velocities along our line of sight, the researchers identified a promising source: IRS 16SW, a massive contact binary system consisting of two stars in extremely close proximity.

According to recent reports, the stellar pair belongs to a disk of young stars that revolves clockwise around Sagittarius A*. Its location and motion provide a plausible explanation for the gas stream. Even the slight differences between the clouds' orbital paths can be accounted for by the movement of the two stars around one another.

Industry observers note that computer simulations of how gas flows and interacts provided additional support for this explanation. The models indicate that powerful stellar winds from the binary system can collide with surrounding material, creating a shock in the region between the stars. Gas then accumulates and becomes compressed, forming dense concentrations that can eventually separate from the system.

Once released, these compact clouds can travel inward along paths resembling those observed in the G1-2-3 streamer. This provides a physical explanation for how one binary star system could produce several distinct clouds moving along closely related orbits.

A Fresh Clue to How Supermassive Black Holes Are Fed.

In a recent development, the findings suggest that massive stars near the Galactic Center may provide a continuing supply of gas capable of fueling Sagittarius A*. Rather than relying only on material already circulating around the black hole, the system could receive fresh gas from the powerful winds generated by nearby stars.

It has been revealed that the discovery also brings together several notable processes in astronomy. The evolution of massive stars, the movement and compression of gas, and the supply of material to supermassive black holes may all be closely connected. By identifying a possible source of the mysterious clouds near Sagittarius A*, researchers have uncovered a latest way in which stars could help sustain black hole activity at the heart of our own galaxy.

Hims & Hers rolls out upcoming peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that hims & Hers Health on Wednesday remarked it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S.
  • Even as it unveiled the newly introduced products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.
  • The upcoming offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hims & Hers Health on Wednesday remarked it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it unveiled the newly introduced products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

The upcoming offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October launched an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a company spokesperson mentioned in a statement.

Sources indicate that none of the firm's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims noted they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy.".

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

According to recent reports, the firm will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

In a recent development, hims said it plans to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The organization also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized initiative to their needs, if appropriate.

The company remarked it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

In a recent development, "If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options.".

However, Vinjamoori mentioned there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

"We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he stated. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a manufacturer of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead.".

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He stated Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight.".

It has been revealed that but health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," said Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body.".

Kritzer mentioned the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Industry observers note that without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, stated Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide users, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler stated one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?".

But he stated the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

It has been revealed that that appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The company notes patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Recent findings suggest that hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that states the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

In practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "significant fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

There is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data demonstrates only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Sources indicate that glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione demonstrated that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also said in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

All of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

Recent findings suggest that google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. Sources indicate that there are some notable differences between each Workspace proposal – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three looks come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.

Google offers four different Workspace prepares, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise strategy.

It has been revealed that although you have access to all the apps regardless of the strategy you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard intends. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That highlights up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this blueprint, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

Most people should use the Standard initiative, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

In a recent development, google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in fresh functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.

Sources indicate that you can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.

Industry observers note that let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to promptly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.

Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

Recent findings suggest that google Workspace Flows is a upcoming tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.

8 Kindle features you should be using.

The Mashable team is split on this question. Our resident Kindle expert Samantha Mangino (yours truly) recommends most people opt for the ad-supported version. However, Mashable Tech Editor Timothy Beck Werth recommends paying a little more to get a Kindle without lockscreen ads. Though this increases the price by $20 to $25, you won't be subjected to annoying ads for books every time you lock your e-reader. Instead, you'll see black-and-white photographs of writing implements and other book motifs.

According to recent reports, when you're buying a Kindle, you'll notice that Amazon selects the "Lockscreen Ad Supported" version by default. Shoppers must manually select "Without Lockscreen Ads" if they want to remove advertisements from the lock screen. This increases the cost of the base Kindle from $149.99 to $169.99; the Kindle Paperwhite increases from $199.99 to $219.99. For serious readers who hate ads, we think it's worth the added cost.

It has been revealed that in the past, the Paperwhite has been Amazon's flagship e-reader, with the Paperwhite Signature Edition being the more luxe option. However, with the 2026 redesign, it seems like the script has been flipped, with Amazon pushing the Signature Edition while the standard Paperwhite takes a back seat.

Plenty remains the same between the devices. They have the same 7-inch screen with 300 ppi resolution and adjustable warmth and brightness. Both are waterproof with IPX8 ratings and 12-week battery life. The new devices also have easy-to-open back panels to make replacing the battery that much easier.

In a recent development, the Paperwhite is the cheaper option at $199.99, but it comes with only 16GB of storage (which, to be fair, is still plenty) and is available in graphite with a plastic casing. The Signature Edition is more expensive at $249.99, but comes with 32GB of storage and is available in the aluminum finish in seaglass green and graphite. Beyond its nicer finish, it also has an ad-free lockscreen, automatic front-light adjustment, a rotating screen, and wireless charging. The real perk of the Paperwhite Signature Edition is its compatibility with the Page Turn Cover, which adds page-turning buttons to your Kindle.

Industry observers note that as of May 20, 2026, Amazon no longer provides software updates or web services to devices released in 2012 or earlier, essentially bricking them. Users will still be able to read presently downloaded books on the device, but to add new books, they will need to connect the device to a computer. This is a huge hit, especially to Libby users who need web service access to read borrowed books.

Kindle Paperwhite (1st generation).

In a recent development, owners of these Kindle models are obviously upset, as it means they'll need to purchase a new device to maintain access to all features. While some are considering switching to a different e-reader, like a Kobo, Amazon still makes great e-readers, and it's a testament to the brand that devices that are at least 14 years old are still going strong.

Unfortunately, while a lot of Amazon devices get regular discounts throughout the year, we only see Kindle discounts during major shopping events like Prime Day and Black Friday. However, even at full price, these devices earn a strong recommendation from Mashable.

Kindle Kids editions come with built-in parental controls. It displays a library geared toward kid-friendly and age-appropriate content. Plus, it allows your kid to request books to read that you have to approve in the Kindle app — that way, you know exactly what they're reading.

Unlike other Kindle models, the Kindle Kids includes a built-in cover and a free one-year Amazon Kids+ subscription that provides access to thousands of books for kids ages 6 to 12. Plus, it comes with a worry-free guarantee: If the Kindle Kids gets damaged within two years of purchase, they'll replace it totally free.

Recent findings suggest that however, any Kindle can technically be a suitable device for kids. When setting up a Kindle, you'll receive a prompt asking if the device is for children, which enables parental controls on it.

Yes, you can buy upcoming Kindles at Best Buy. However, if you're searching for the best price and a convenient shopping experience, we recommend sticking with Amazon. Since the Kindle store is also hosted at Amazon, you'll need an account there anyway, and it's hard to beat Amazon's prices on its own products.

I made sure to pinpoint which models are waterproof for a worry-free outdoor reading experience as well as those better suited for children.

Kindle models vary wildly in price; I made sure to include an affordable Kindle as well as splurge-worthy, treat-yourself picks.

This includes auto-adjusting displays for indoor/outdoor reading, warm light settings to block blue light, and page turn buttons for one-handed reading.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.
  • The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anticipating flood of Democratic requests, US president problems executive order in attempt to stymie oversight efforts.

Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order claims. If they fail to comply, the White House warns, their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

In a recent development, the order signed late Friday is the administration’s latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump’s family, particularly at the Pentagon.

It comes as White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations once Democrats take power in January.

On Monday, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, told US agencies that they must seek approval from his office and the White House’s office of legislative affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to the US representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to “blatant criminality”.

Garcia earlier this week sent letters directing members of Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach”, arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government”.

According to recent reports, presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.

Friday’s executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the automaker mentioned Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

It has been revealed that the automaker mentioned Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

According to recent reports, the production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

It has been revealed that the automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

It has been revealed that alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, noted licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

Sources indicate that "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

According to recent reports, in September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Sources indicate that ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the organization's energy storage business. That's down from initial looks of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford noted it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it prepares to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.
